Where it began

Shaun Pollock was born on 16 July 1973 in Gqeberha. Cricket ran in the family: his grandfather Andrew, born in Edinburgh, had played for Orange Free State.

He went to Northwood School in Durban and later took a commerce degree at the University of Natal, so whatever happened on the field, the numbers off it were in safe hands.

The player

He was a bowling all-rounder, and for years he shared the new ball with Allan Donald in one of the great South African partnerships. His Test career ran from 1995 to 2008 and took in 108 matches. He took 421 wickets at 23.12, with 16 five-wicket innings and a best of 7 for 87, and he added 3,781 runs at 32.32, including two hundreds and 16 fifties.

He led South Africa from April 2000 until 2003, in 26 Tests, of which they won 14 and lost only five. In 1998 he helped South Africa lift the ICC KnockOut Trophy, their first ICC title. When he retired, only five other men had reached 3,000 runs and 300 wickets in Tests, and no South African had more Test wickets until Dale Steyn passed him in December 2018.

What made him special

Accuracy was his gift. Batsmen found almost nothing loose to hit. When he finished, no bowler with 300 one-day wickets had given away runs more slowly, and nobody had bowled more maidens in one-day internationals than his 313.

With the bat he was a lower-order man who refused to behave like one. His two Test hundreds both came from number nine or lower, a record of its own. Hundreds in one-day cricket took him longer to find: 189 innings, a record of patience, before the first one came. He was also the first Test captain to be left unbeaten on 99, which is one way to make sure people remember an innings.

Away from the middle

He played county cricket for Warwickshire, and in his very first game for them, in 1996, he took wickets with four balls running. He later turned out for Durham and for the Mumbai Indians. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 2003, South Africa gave him the Order of Ikhamanga in Silver, and in November 2021 he joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame. After he stopped playing he became a familiar voice on SuperSport and at the major ICC tournaments.

And finally

In 2007, playing for an Africa XI as a specialist batsman, he made 130 from number seven, the highest score from that position in a one-day international. MS Dhoni beat it later in the same series, so the record was his only briefly. All the same, not bad for a man who was mainly there to bowl.
